title: Does an Executable Validator Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated Network Configuration Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow. Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the identical candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; paired contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We expand methodological detail, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, reproducibility guidance grounded in archived artifacts, and discuss construct/external validity limits and design recommendations for future confirmatory studies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) promise to translate operator intent into concrete network configuration commands, potentially improving NetOps productivity. However, syntactically plausible commands can violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing hazardous uplink switchover), causing semantic failures only visible in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Evaluating guarded pipelines requires executable tests that detect semantic and stateful failures beyond token- or syntax-level correctness.

We executed a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that isolates the marginal effect of an executable validator and a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. The central confirmatory research question was: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: each task produced one generator output that was scored both as baseline (LLM-only) and as guarded (validator±repair). This design removes generator-induced variability across paired episodes and directly measures validator/repair influence on identical candidates.

Our contribution is a fully preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) that holds the generator fixed and measures the incremental effect of an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy, together with complete execution accounting, deterministic reconciliation, representative diagnostics, and concrete recommendations for follow-up confirmatory designs when generators produce few invalid candidates.
sections.related_work:
Two complementary research strands frame this study. Executable-benchmark and NetOps verification work (for example, recent executable benchmarks and emulation-grounded evaluations) emphasize that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: closed-loop emulation exposes sequencing and stateful errors—make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, and required-ordered operations—that simple syntactic checks miss. A second strand explores tool-augmented LLM agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) as operational safety measures. Survey and benchmark reports consistently recommend integrating verification or emulation; however, cross-model closed-loop comparisons under identical harnesses and designs that isolate validator effects are limited.

Our approach complements these efforts by using a shared-generation paired design to isolate validator/repair marginal effects for identical generator outputs. This contrasts with prior studies that conflate generator variability with verification efficacy and highlights the different experimental lenses—generator-focused vs validator-focused—needed to understand where safety gains arise in agentic NetOps pipelines.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified test was the exact two-sided McNemar. A bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was included for the paired-difference estimate. The preregistration also defined exclusion/contamination rules, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, and sensitivity analyses (e.g., treating technical exclusions as failures).

Task generation and structured payload. Tasks were produced deterministically by a domain-specific task generator. Each task payload encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, a required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level). Including an explicit required_sequence allowed the emulator validator to check sequencing and workflow policies as structured constraints rather than relying on heuristic text matching.

Shared-generation design and rationale. For each paired task we performed a single shared initial candidate generation using the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini). This shared-candidate design isolates the marginal effect of the validator and repair subsystem by removing generator variance across paired episodes. The trade-off is that if the generator systematically produces valid candidates for the selected task bank, repair is unused—an anticipated risk discussed in the preregistration.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0), an executable state checker that applied task-encoded workflow policies (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator executed the candidate in emulated state, emitting a structured validator_trace that records validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and an explicit repair_applied flag. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one repair iteration when violation_count>0; repair prompts and any provider traces were to be archived when generated. In this execution, violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and no repair artifacts were produced.

Instrumentation, contamination controls, and deterministic reconciliation. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets between tasks and recorded provider-call audits and contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse). The run completed with no contamination flags and no technical exclusions. Core execution accounting numbers are: planned_episode_count = 240 (120 pairs × 2 conditions), completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair), and maximum_model_calls planned = 240. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed pair accounting and provider-audit consistency (concordant pairs n_11=120; no cross-condition cache reuse observed).

Statistical analysis and degenerate-interval clarification. The primary test is exact two-sided McNemar on paired binary pass/fail labels per task. The bootstrap-percentile CI was computed by resampling paired outcomes (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). When the empirical contingency table contains zero discordant pairs (n_10 = n_01 = 0), all bootstrap resamples reproduce the same paired table and produce identical paired-difference values; hence the percentile CI is degenerate (lower = upper = observed difference). This degenerate CI is an exact consequence of the observed concordant data under the preregistered resampling scheme and parameters, not an implementation error.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions. Condition-level summaries report baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0, guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes.

Per-topology outcomes (explicit counts). The preregistered deterministic task partition produced 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology results are:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40 success; guarded = 40/40 success.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40 success; guarded = 40/40 success.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40 success; guarded = 40/40 success.

Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring and validator traces show normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count equals required_command_count from the task payload, validator.validation_after.valid = true, and validator.repair_applied = false. Example task payloads include required_sequence entries (e.g., shutdown→configure→restore, make-before-break uplink switchover, dual-down MTU change) that the validator enforces as structured checks; archived traces show these canonical constraints were satisfied by the generator output under the frozen prompt strategy.

Repair activity and secondary endpoints. Because validator.violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the run and no repair-provider-call artifacts exist. Preregistered secondary endpoints that quantify repair incidence and repair-call counts are vacuous in this execution; the absence of repair activity is an empirical observation recorded in validator traces and in the deterministic reconciliation.

Contamination, missingness, and reconciliation. Contamination heuristics did not flag any episodes and missingness summaries report complete_pairs = 120 with zero technical exclusions. Deterministic reconciliation confirms provider-audit counts and pair accounting are internally consistent, supporting the integrity of the confirmatory statistics reported above.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design was chosen to answer a narrowly scoped mechanistic question—can a validator/repair subsystem improve outcomes for identical generator outputs? In this archived task bank and under the declared generator/prompt configuration the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling outcome.

Design trade-offs and concrete recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but may under-exercise repair when the generator is well-calibrated for the chosen task bank. Based on recorded task-manifest difficulty metadata and the absence of repairs, we recommend the following preregistered design adjustments for future confirmatory runs intended to measure repair utility:
1) Independent generation per condition: allow separate generator draws per condition so guarded pipelines can intercept generator errors that arise from prompt or sampling variability; account for paired blocking where appropriate.
2) Controlled prompt perturbations: apply systematic perturbations to prompts on a prespecified subset to increase generator error incidence while keeping other blocks paired to preserve internal controls.
3) Task stratification: concentrate confirmatory power on tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count to increase probability of generator-induced violations and exercise repair.
4) Expanded repair budget for exploratory arms: allow multiple repair iterations in exploratory arms to measure repair convergence behavior and repair-call costs.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (checked rules, touched fields, why repair was not applied) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. Instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) supports operator-facing explanations and third-party audits in deployments where generators sometimes err. The experiment also underlines that claims about repair benefits require careful experimental framing: if generators rarely produce invalid candidates under a given prompt, the guard will be idle by design.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator's policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; while required_sequence enforces canonical workflows, the validator does not emulate all vendor-specific behaviors or partial-observability telemetry. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure ≈ 0.40 and targeted absolute reduction 0.15; observed baseline = 0.00 violates those assumptions and makes the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and illustrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
